newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ tax issues face delay as Govt settles in.
newsitem.headline: NZ tax issues face delay as Govt settles in.

text.p: Reports on four tax policy issues the Inland Revenue Department classified as "immediate" and requiring attention over the next six months have been delayed, a spokesman for Revenue Minister Bill Birch said on Thursday.

In briefing papers to the incoming government released on Thursday but prepared before the October 12, 1996 election Inland Revenue said discussion documents on rules governing the cost of trading stock, tax on overseas income of non-residents and the design and implications of a carbon tax would all be released in December.
The department said a joint government and private sector working party on the options for taxing life office and superannuation fund savings would also report back in December.
But a spokesman for Revenue Minister Bill Birch said it had been announced in December that the report on trading stock and tax conduiting would be delayed until sometime this year.
The other reports had also been delayed.
Another spokesman for Birch said no dates had been placed on further action on the reports, but that no significance should be read into that.

"It is just the consideration of the coalition document and getting new people into place... There is no significance in the delays. They are just part of the complications of getting the new (government) up and running," he said.
The tax policy contained in the coalition agreement makes no specific mention of the four issues in question.
In its briefing Inland Revenue said taxing non-residents on their overseas income could make New Zealand unattractive as a base for companies' regional headquarters.
The government has said it will introduce a low-level carbon charge in December 1997 if by June New Zealand was not on track to achieve its carbon dioxide emission target by the year 2000.
Former Revenue Minister, United MP Peter Dunne, has called on the government to delay its timeframe for the carbon tax to allow a wider public debate.

The coalition agreement makes no mention of a carbon tax but says: "Every effort will be made to ensure the implementation of a coherent plan to reduce gross CO2 emissions and make significant progress towards meeting international obligations." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
